purpose: Melatonin is mainly used to help you fall asleep, especially if you have trouble with your sleep schedule, like from jet lag or shift work. It can also help people who just have difficulty falling asleep at night. Unlike many sleep aids, it is available without a prescription.
how_it_works: Your body naturally makes melatonin in a small gland in your brain when it gets dark outside — it is basically your body's signal that it is time to sleep. Taking melatonin as a supplement adds to what your body already makes, helping to tell your brain it is time to wind down and get sleepy. It does not knock you out like a strong sedative; it gently nudges your internal clock in the right direction.
common_side_effects: Most people tolerate melatonin well, but some may feel drowsy or groggy the next morning. Other possible side effects include headache, dizziness, nausea, and feeling a little moody or irritable. These are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Because it makes you sleepy, avoid driving or operating heavy machinery after taking it. Talk to your doctor before using it if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or taking blood thinners, seizure medications, or medications that suppress the immune system. Children should only use it under a doctor's guidance. If you have an autoimmune condition or diabetes, check with your doctor first, as melatonin may affect blood sugar and immune function.
typical_dosing: For most adults, a low dose of 0.5 mg to 5 mg taken 30 to 60 minutes before bedtime is a good starting point. Many people think more is better, but lower doses often work just as well. Take the smallest dose that helps you sleep. For jet lag, take it at your destination's bedtime for a few nights to help reset your internal clock.
